answer.rationale: The binding constraints eliminate most paths: negotiate_terms is already foreclosed (incumbent refused to reopen price), renew_incumbent alone cannot meet an 18% cut, and defer_decision is unavailable in substance because the contract does not auto-renew while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. That leaves a cost move against a hard delivery-risk ceiling. memory_c2 is the single memory that would justify a wholesale switch to the low-cost vendor, so it is the one worth pulling: I need the original record to know what it actually covered. If that cost win came on a low-volume or non-critical part with slack in the line, it does not transfer to a primary contract at 94% utilization with a 14-day runway, and a full switch would be an unhedged bet on onboarding speed. Note also that memory_c2 reports cost and invoicing accuracy only \u2014 it is silent on defect rates, spec conformance, and delivery reliability under load, which is exactly the information a cost-driven switch turns on. Its quick onboarding may reflect an easy scope rather than vendor capability. So I intend a guarded dual-source: qualify the low-cost vendor on a bounded share of volume while holding the incumbent as primary on a short extension, which is the structure memory_c3 records as having held allocation through a shortage. This captures partial savings toward the mandate and buys optionality on a full switch next review without betting the line. Explicit risks: this likely lands short of 18% this cycle, and split volume may forfeit the incumbent's volume pricing described in memory_c6, so total cost of ownership could move the wrong way if the discount cliff is steep. I am also flagging the downstream value risk that an 18% spend mandate pushes toward selecting on price against unverified quality and reliability, where a field failure in industrial hardware costs far more than the savings. Qualification gates should be conformance and on-time delivery under load, not unit price alone.
